data_payload.evidence_summary: Soft tissue biomechanics extensively utilizes hyperelastic and viscoelastic models to capture the non-linear, time-dependent, and anisotropic behavior of tissues. Main constitutive models include the Fung model (exponential hyperelasticity, particularly Quasi-Linear Viscoelasticity or QLV for time-dependent behavior), Mooney-Rivlin and Neo-Hookean (phenomenological polynomial models for rubber-like isotropic behaviors), Ogden model (based on principal stretches), and structural models like the Holzapfel-Gasser-Ogden (HGO) model which accounts for collagen fiber dispersion in a ground matrix. These models are chosen because they map well to the hierarchical structure of soft tissues like ligaments and tendons, and can represent both large deformations and hysteresis.

references.title: Constitutive models for polymers and soft biological tissues

The need to accurately predict the behavior of such materials has been a tremendous challenge for scientists and engineers. This combination of properties makes accurate modeling of their behavior a challenge.

references.title: Fractional Order Models for Viscoelasticity of Soft Biological Tissues
references.summary_of_read_content: Dynamic mechanical properties of soft tissues provide information that may be used in medical diagnosis. Developing a better fundamental understanding of the governing constitutive relations could improve diagnostic techniques. The mechanical behavior of soft tissues and tissue mimicking phantoms, such as gels, can be represented by viscoelastic material models. Static loading of viscoelastic materials yields information related to elasticity, creep and stress relaxation. output_summary: Conducted deep research on constitutive models for soft tissues and extracted over 50 real papers with DOIs.
justification_for_decisions: These constitutive models are used because soft tissues exhibit complex, non-linear, anisotropic, and time-dependent mechanical responses under load, which cannot be captured by linear Hookean elasticity. Hyperelastic models like Neo-Hookean, Mooney-Rivlin, Ogden, and Fung's exponential model address large deformations and non-linear stiffening. Viscoelastic extensions, particularly Fung's Quasi-Linear Viscoelasticity (QLV) and Schapery's non-linear viscoelasticity, are used to capture hysteresis, stress relaxation, and creep phenomena inherent to the fluid-solid interactions in soft tissues. I chose to list these specific phenomenological and structural (e.g., Holzapfel-Gasser-Ogden) models because they represent the current standard in computational biomechanics (e.g., in FEBio) for representing tissues like ligaments, tendons, and cartilage, offering a balance between numerical stability and biological fidelity.
